structure.title: CHAPTER II
key_items: CONSTITUTION OF CRIMINAL COURTS AND OFFICES
structure.summary:
**Chapter II – Constitution of Criminal Courts and Offices**  
The chapter establishes the hierarchy of criminal courts in each state—Sessions Courts, Judicial Magistrates (first and second class), and Executive Magistrates—detailing that magistrate functions are divided between judicial and executive roles, that all offences (under the Sanhita or other laws) are to be investigated and tried under its provisions, and that state governments may adjust divisions and districts with High Court consultation.

structure.title: CHAPTER III
structure.summary: **Summary:** Chapter III establishes the hierarchy and duties of the Directorate of Prosecution, with the Director overseeing serious offences (≥10 years, life, death), the Deputy Director handling offences punishable 7–10 years, and the Assistant Director managing offences punishable <7 years; all prosecutors are subordinate to these officers, who may also oversee all proceedings under the Sanhita, except the Advocate General.

structure.title: CHAPTER IV
key_items: POWERS OF SUPERIOR OFFICERS OF POLICE AND AID TO THE MAGISTRATES AND THE POLICE
structure.summary:
**Chapter IV – Powers of Superior Police Officers and Assistance to Magistrates**  
This chapter grants superior‑ranked police officers the authority to exercise the same powers as the officer in charge of a station across their entire local area, allows magistrates and police to withdraw or transfer such powers, and requires every person to assist a magistrate or police officer in arrests, maintaining peace, or preventing injury to public property, with additional provisions for executing warrants and determining successors in office.

structure.title: CHAPTER V
structure.summary:
**CHAPTER V – ARREST OF PERSONS**  
Police may arrest without a magistrate’s order or warrant any person who commits a cognizable offence in their presence, or who is reasonably suspected of such an offence (punishable up to 7 years or more, including death penalty) based on complaint, credible information, or suspicion, provided the officer believes the arrest is necessary to prevent further crime, ensure investigation, safeguard evidence, or compel court appearance; the officer must record written reasons for arrest or non‑arrest.

structure.title: CHAPTER VI
structure.summary:
**Chapter VI – Processes to Compel Appearance**  
This chapter sets out the rules for issuing, signing, and serving court summons (including electronic forms), the requirement that a person arrested by police be released only on bond or a magistrate’s order, the authority to pursue escaped detainees, and the general prohibition against arrests outside the law.

structure.title: CHAPTER VII
structure.summary: **Chapter VII** covers court‑issued processes: it sets out how summonses are issued to compel appearance, the use of search‑warrants and general search provisions, and miscellaneous rules for executing warrants, including arrest warrants, property attachment, sale, and appeal rights.

structure.title: CHAPTER VIII
structure.summary:
**Chapter VIII – Reciprocal Arrangements for Assistance in Criminal Matters**  
This section allows a court to serve or execute summons, arrest warrants, or search warrants issued by courts in other Indian states or in contracting foreign states, treating them as if issued locally; it sets procedures for handling arrests and searches, and requires forwarding seized documents or items back to the issuing court under central government notification.

structure.title: CHAPTER IX
key_items: SECURITY FOR KEEPING THE PEACE AND FOR GOOD BEHAVIOUR
structure.summary:
**Chapter IX – Security for Keeping the Peace and Good Behaviour**  
The chapter allows a Court of Session or first‑class magistrate to order a convicted person (or abettor) to post a bond or bail for up to three years to maintain peace, covering offences punishable under Chapter XI (except certain sections), assault, mischief, criminal intimidation, and other related offences. It also sets procedures for revoking forfeiture orders, handling property transfers, and transmitting requests or warrants between the Central Government and contracting states.

structure.title: CHAPTER X
structure.summary:
**Chapter X – Order for Detention and Bond Cancellation**  
This section governs the remand of a person to prison for the unexpired portion of a conditional discharge, allowing release upon giving new security; it permits courts or magistrates to cancel bonds for good behaviour, and requires that when a summoned person appears, the bond be cancelled and fresh security be provided for the remaining term.

structure.title: CHAPTER XI

nodes.title: C. —Urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

structure.summary:
**Chapter XI – Maintenance of Public Order and Tranquillity**  
This chapter empowers executive magistrates and police officers to command and, if necessary, forcibly disperse unlawful assemblies or any gathering of five or more persons likely to disturb public peace, with the option to involve armed forces for larger or obstinate groups. It also covers the handling of public nuisances, urgent nuisance or danger cases, and disputes over immovable property, outlining procedures for maintaining order and protecting public safety.

structure.title: CHAPTER XII
structure.summary: **Summary:** Chapter XII empowers police to take preventive action against cognizable offences: officers may arrest suspects without a warrant if the offence cannot otherwise be stopped, must report designs to superiors, and can detain suspects up to 24 hours unless further authority is granted. The chapter also allows officers to interpose to protect public property and mandates compliance with lawful police directions.

structure.title: CHAPTER XIII
key_items: INFORMATION TO THE POLICE AND THEIR POWERS TO INVESTIGATE
structure.summary: **Summary:** Chapter XIII outlines police powers for preventive action and local inquiries: officers may investigate and arrest without a warrant when a cognizable offence is imminent, must act within 24 hours of arrest, and can interpose to protect public property; magistrates may deputize subordinates for inquiries, direct cost payments, and use inquiry reports as evidence.

structure.title: CHAPTER XIV
key_items: JURISDICTION OF THE CRIMINAL COURTS IN INQUIRIES AND TRIALS
structure.summary:
**Chapter XIV – Jurisdiction of Criminal Courts in Inquiries and Trials**  
The chapter establishes that every offence is normally investigated and tried by the court having local jurisdiction where it was committed, but allows a court with jurisdiction over any of several relevant local areas to take over when the offence’s location is uncertain, spans multiple areas, or involves continuing or related acts. It also outlines procedural provisions for magistrate‑led inquiries, evidence recording, post‑mortem examinations, and notifying relatives.

structure.title: CHAPTER XV
key_items: CONDITIONS REQUISITE FOR INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS
structure.summary:
**Chapter XV Summary**  
This chapter governs how offences committed outside a magistrate’s jurisdiction—or outside India—are initiated and processed: a first‑class magistrate may investigate and compel appearance for such offences as if committed locally, or take bail if the offence is not capital; if multiple magistrates are involved, the High Court decides; offences by Indian citizens abroad or by non‑citizens on Indian‑registered vessels/aircraft are treated as if committed in India, but require prior Central Government sanction; the Central Government may also direct the receipt of foreign depositions or exhibits as evidence in Indian courts.

structure.title: CHAPTER XVI
structure.summary:
**Chapter XVI – Complaints to Magistrates**  
Magistrates must examine complainants and witnesses on oath, record the examination, and give the accused a chance to be heard; written complaints by public servants or courts need not be re‑examined, and cases may be transferred under §212. Complaints against public servants in the discharge of duty require the servant’s assertions and a superior’s report before cognizance is taken. If a magistrate lacks jurisdiction, he must return the complaint (written) or direct the complainant to the proper court. A magistrate may postpone issuing process for an accused outside his area, conduct an inquiry or direct investigation to determine whether to proceed.

structure.title: CHAPTER XVII
structure.summary:
**Chapter XVII – Commencement of Proceedings Before Magistrates**  
The chapter sets out how a magistrate may initiate criminal proceedings: dismissing a complaint if no ground exists, issuing summons or warrants (including electronically) only after a witness list is filed, attaching the complaint to any summons, and requiring payment of fees before process issuance. It allows the accused to appear by counsel or personally, with the magistrate retaining discretion to enforce personal attendance, and provides for summary disposal of petty offences with a summons to the accused.

structure.title: CHAPTER XVIII
structure.summary:
**Chapter XVIII – The Charge**  
This chapter sets out the form and content of criminal charges, requiring each charge to state the specific offence, its legal basis, and any necessary definition so the accused is fully notified; it also governs the joinder of multiple charges and provides illustrative examples.

structure.title: CHAPTER XIX
key_items: TRIAL BEFORE A COURT OF SESSION
structure.summary:
**Chapter XIX – Trial Before a Court of Session**  
This chapter mandates that all trials before a Court of Session be prosecuted by a Public Prosecutor, who must open the case by stating the charge and the evidence to be presented. It also allows the accused to apply for discharge within 60 days of appearance, and provides procedures for withdrawing or staying charges if a conviction on one head is obtained.

nodes.title: A. —Cases instituted on a police report
nodes.summary: Section 260 governs cases instituted on a police report: it requires that a Court of Session try such cases under the warrant‑case procedure, may hold the trial in camera, and mandates that the alleged victim be examined as a witness unless the court directs otherwise. If the accused are discharged or acquitted, the court may order the alleged victim (except high officials) to pay up to ₹5,000 in compensation to the accused, treating it as a fine, while allowing appeal and ensuring the payment counts toward any later civil suit.

nodes.title: B. —Cases instituted otherwise than on police report
nodes.summary:
**Summary:**  
Section 263 allows a magistrate to frame a written charge within 60 days if he believes an offence is likely, after hearing the accused and offering a plea. If the accused pleads guilty, the magistrate may convict (§264). If not, the magistrate schedules witness examination, provides the accused with police statements, may summon witnesses, and permits audio‑video evidence; the accused then presents his defence and may request processes to compel witnesses or documents, subject to the magistrate’s discretion.

nodes.title: C. —Conclusion of trial
nodes.summary: **Conclusion of trial** – The Magistrate may discharge the accused if evidence shows no case for conviction, or if the charge is groundless at any stage. If the Magistrate believes the accused committed a triable offence, he frames a written charge, reads it to the accused, and allows a guilty plea or a defense; the accused may cross‑examine prosecution witnesses, after which witnesses are discharged, and the trial proceeds with the remaining evidence.

structure.title: CHAPTER XXX

nodes.title: SUBMISSION OF DEATH SENTENCES FOR CONFIRMATION

structure.summary:
**CHAPTER XXX – Confirmation of Death Sentences**  
When a Court of Session sentences a person to death, the case is immediately submitted to the High Court, which may confirm the sentence, alter it, annul the conviction, or order a new trial, and may conduct further inquiry or evidence; the High Court’s decision requires at least two judges’ signatures and must wait until any appeal period expires. The chapter also covers the procedures for appeals, reference, and revision of such sentences.

structure.title: CHAPTER XXXIII

nodes.title: EXECUTION, SUSPENSION, REMISSION AND COMMUTATION OF SENTENCES; A. —Death sentences
key_items: EXECUTION, SUSPENSION, REMISSION AND COMMUTATION OF SENTENCES

nodes.title: E. —Suspension, remission and commutation of sentences

structure.summary:
**Chapter XXXIII – Transfer of Criminal Cases**  
This chapter empowers the Supreme Court and High Courts to transfer criminal cases, appeals, or classes of cases between courts of equal or superior jurisdiction when justice, impartiality, or legal complexity demands it, and allows High Courts to direct trials to other courts or themselves; it also provides for compensation against frivolous applications.

structure.title: THE FIRST SCHEDULE
key_items: I. —OFFENCES UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA
II. —CLASSIFICATION OF OFFENCES AGAINST OTHER LAWS
structure.summary: The First Schedule classifies offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, indicating that the listed punishments are only indicative of the offence’s substance, not the exact penalty. It specifies that “Magistrate of the first class” excludes executive magistrates, defines “cognizable” as arrest without warrant, and “non‑cognizable” as requiring a warrant, and then details the nature (cognizable/non‑cognizable, bailable/non‑bailable, triable court) and corresponding punishment for various abetment offences.

structure.title: THE SECOND SCHEDULE
structure.summary: **Summary:** The Second Schedule provides standard police and court forms for criminal procedure: Form No. 1 is a police notice for appearance under section 35(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, directing an accused to appear at a specified time and place; Form No. 2 is a summons under section 63, requiring an accused to appear before a magistrate to answer a specified charge.

structure.title: WHERE A BOND WITH SURETIES IS TO BE EXECUTED, ADD—
structure.summary: **Summary:** The section provides the format and requirements for a bond of appearance for an offender released pending fine payment, including the offender’s commitment to appear before the court and forfeiture of a specified sum if defaulting, and the additional clause for sureties who must jointly and severally guarantee the offender’s appearance and pay the forfeiture if the offender defaults.
